notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg072.1st1K-gr: 'The Asclepiadeans' renders οἱ Ἀσκληπιάδαι, taken here as the followers of Asclepiades, not physicians of the Asclepiad clan. In 1.1 οἷοι πολλοὶ τῶν μετ’ αὐτῶν ('many of those after them') is translated as if μετ’ αὐτόν ('after him'), the sense being after Hippocrates. In 1.1 ὑφ’ ἡμῶν βλεπόμενος in 2.1 reads literally 'seen by us', which does not fit the sentence; the passage is translated 'seen by you', assuming the text should read ὑφ’ ὑμῶν. In 2.1 τολμήσῃς is an unusual form after ὅταν... ἴδῃς and is taken as an ironic command ('dare'). The sentence ἐπεὶ δ’ ἄνθρωπος... is incomplete in the Greek; '[I am]' supplies the sense. Scanning errors silently corrected: ὑδατω δῶν, ἀνα τρέπονται.

At 3.1, ἡμετέραν σοφίαν ("our wisdom") is translated as printed, but it may be ironic or an error for ὑμετέραν ("your wisdom"). Also at 3.1, ᾧ δῆλον ὡς ("From this it is clear") reads awkwardly and the text may be corrupt. At 3.1, βδάλλοντα ("things that suck") is uncertain; the reference may be to suckling animals or leeches. At 4.1, πηξάσης τῆς γαστρός ("his belly seized up") is uncertain: it may mean cramp or some urgent bowel trouble. At 5.1, the printed full stop after μόνῃ καθάρσει splits one sentence, and the translation reads straight through it. The syntax of ἐπηρεάσοντας ... Ἱπποκράτην is compressed, and the rendering given is an interpretation. The "elephants" are presumably elephantiasis. Galen does not name the plant in the Bithynian story.

nodes.text: Galen, On the Power of Purgative Drugs.

It seems that the most ancient physicians left bad opinions unrefuted for the same reason that the earliest lawgivers left the greatest crimes unpunished. For since wickedness was more moderate in that time, and people neither attempted the greatest injustices nor brought themselves to the most blatant shamelessness, how could anyone have either fixed a punishment for things that had never happened at all, or brought a refutation against things that no one had said at all? But when, as wickedness grew over time, there was no longer anything that people would not dare or would not say, the lawgivers devised many new kinds of punishment for wrongdoers, and those who honour truth [devised] many kinds of refutation against the sophists. This is what I too now seem likely to do, in refuting those who do away with the power of purgative drugs to attract the humours they evacuate, and who claim instead that they have a power of changing all that comes near them, all alike. Hippocrates said nothing against such an opinion. For neither Asclepiades existed in his day, who openly behaved without shame and stripped, as it were, for a contest against the truth, nor Erasistratus, who with a certain modesty, indeed, yet overturned the whole main point that plainly holds concerning purgative drugs. For nowhere in his writings does Erasistratus recognise the attractive power, the most effective and most proper power of nature; instead he uses in its place the following toward what is being emptied. But the power in purgative drugs is a part of the power that attracts what is proper to it, just as is the power by which bile and urine are separated out, and many other things accomplished by nature, both in the health of animals and in the cures of diseases and in the diseases themselves, by physicians and not least by nature herself. Since, then, Hippocrates said nothing against those who abolish attraction from existence, because the doctrine did not yet have so reckless a champion as many of those after him proved to be, it would be right for us to contend for the truth in place of Hippocrates, and first to remind [the reader] what sort of thing these men say, and next to show that they do not speak correctly. Their argument, then, is as follows. The purgative drug alters whatever humour it touches into its own form: it produces yellow bile, in the drug they call cholagogue, and likewise phlegm, in the one they call phlegmagogue; it creates a watery substance, in the one they call hydragogue; and another renders whatever humour it touches black bile. In short, what is called purging is a change and alteration of all the humours in the veins, not an evacuation of one of them, according to their argument. But if this is what you want, let us now say to them that, whether someone takes a drug that draws off bile, or phlegm, or black [bile], or a whey-like fluid, all the humours are evacuated from the veins. And then purging someone with such a drug differs from emptying the blood by cutting a vein only in this: in phlebotomies it is discharged just as it was present before, whereas in purgings it is changed not only in colour but also in consistency. For the drug that draws off watery matter makes everything in the veins fluid and thin, even if it happened previously to be very thick, while the drug that draws off black [bile], on the contrary, makes everything thick and stagnant, even if it was very fluid before. And so our choice between phlebotomising and purging will depend on certain other aims, but it will not depend on the kind of matter being evacuated. What other aims are these? Many people are more ready for phlebotomy than others, and some for purging, just as still others would sooner suffer anything at all than be phlebotomised. And some would rather endure having a part of the body cut off than swallow a drug. Moreover, some have their stomach upset by purgative drugs, while others take them without distress. On the basis of such aims, then, we shall phlebotomise some people and give the purgative drug to others, and not on the grounds that the Asclepiadeans believed, who held that phlebotomy evacuates all the humours in the veins alike, but purging not alike, rather that one humour alone which the drug is said to draw off. That is also why they say the blood is purified by such drugs, not emptied as in phlebotomies. This follows from your hypotheses, whether you will or not.

I shall remind [you] of their main points. According to the Asclepiadeans, the evacuation in phlebotomies is equal for all the humours in the veins, but that in purgings is not equal: rather it is a removal of the others, so as to render the blood pure. According to the followers of Erasistratus, the evacuation of all [the humours] is equal in purgings just as in phlebotomies, and they will say that these are not truly purgings at all, but evacuations together with corruption and alteration of what is evacuated. So now that they have come to the contest, let the moderately shameless among the sophists and the utterly shameless contend with me, as in a stadium, not with words or long drivel, but with the deeds themselves, to which I challenge them in this most populous city, where thousands suffering from jaundice can be found every day, and thousands with dropsy. It is enough for me to discuss these first. Let someone bring me one of these, without fever, whose whole body is full of bitter bile, and let him watch how, after preparing the man for some days, when the moment seems right to me, I give him one of the cholagogue purgatives and from this purging restore the man to his natural state, without doing anything further at all to his body. We have demonstrated this not once or twice, but very often, to those of them who are half depraved, and we have won many over to better views. Yet not for this reason, sophist, do I bid you trust the witnesses, but rather to see for yourself, whenever you wish, the jaundiced man recovering his natural colour with a single purging. So when you see this happen, my noble friend, dare to stand in the middle and, raising your bright voice like a herald, to stretch out a long speech, such as you often give your pupils, to the effect that what is proper to each purgative is not attracted by it, but that everything contained in the veins, whatever its kind, is changed into whatever the power of the drug is naturally able to alter it. And [say] that this man now cured of jaundice benefited not from the evacuation of the humour, but from the general principle of evacuation. 'Watch, then, how I shall benefit in the same way another man in this condition, either by phlebotomising him or by giving him some other purgative.' Having said this, take two of the jaundiced men in succession before me, and phlebotomise the one, and evacuate the other by some such purgative, one that all people [believe] evacuates black bile, but that you are convinced does not evacuate it but generates it. And then, if you benefit him and render his body of good colour, I shall grant you whatever you wish me to suffer; but if you do the man no good, and instead bring him to the extreme of harm, go over to better views and emulate the art of Hippocrates. But enough about the jaundiced. Move on to the man with dropsy and observe again that he too is not affected in the same way by phlebotomy and by one of the hydragogue drugs. For if I do not show that the watery matter in the lower belly is evacuated by the drug, then you may condemn the ancient doctrine, which holds that such a humour is not generated, as you claim, but drawn out of the body by the drug. And do whatever you wish against me. Moreover, if you give a drug that draws off black or yellow bile, you will not evacuate the swelling, and so each of the drugs attracts a certain humour proper to it. But if you think that all [the humours] are altered alike and that what occurs is a common evacuation, not a purging, you are free to cut the vein. If someone had issued this challenge in writing while living among the Indians, it would be hard to refute him. But since [I am] a man seen by you every day, and one who challenges you to the very refutation by deeds, I do not know how you are not ashamed of your babbling. I am not going to say that I have purged the bodies of a great many jaundiced people of the bilious humour with a single purging, for thousands bear witness to this; but if the most shameless sophists pretend to disbelieve everyone, let them watch the deed itself being done, as often as they wish.

And yet why do I say "let them watch"? For I have already shown them this many times, and I remember someone taking hold of even such a piece of idle chatter as this. For he said that it is not one particular kind of humour that is attracted by each of the drugs, but that each of them simply attracts, like things that suck. And that in response to the attraction the thinner part of the humours follows first, after it the thicker, and then finally the thickest. So with the drugs whose strength gives out more quickly, the evacuation stops at the watery matter; with those whose strength lasts longer, yellow bile too is evacuated; and those that are strongest draw out the black as well. At the time, then, this fellow seemed to his devotees to be speaking well, and they all cheered him, and he left us and made off at a great run, knowing for certain, I think, that if he stayed he would be refuted. But when on the following day we gave his chorus a book containing a refutation of what he had so suddenly ventured to say, he was never again as persuasive even to those same people, since he was at a loss to resolve the objections put forward. For this was written in the book: "Yesterday you ran away from the argument, doing something like a competitor who snatches the crown and flees before competing, but today you will not escape refutation. For this book will follow you, once it falls into the hands of your chorus. For the argument is addressed no less to them than to you, since they had never before heard you grant that there is attraction in any existing thing at all, but yesterday heard you agree that all the contents of the veins are attracted together by the drug. For they ought, far from admiring or in any way praising what was said, to have taken it for a betrayal of what you laid down from the beginning. For on the separation of urine and of yellow and black bile, and on many other activities in the body, you all deliver a great many discourses on every occasion, granting anything rather than that attraction of what is proper to it is a natural activity of each body; yet now you have granted not only that attraction exists, but that it is an attraction of absolutely everything, which is a far greater admission than saying it is of what is proper. For that, just as there is in animals a certain power of separating out what is foreign, so too each existing thing has a certain power of attracting what is proper to it, seems reasonable to all people who are not yet wise in our wisdom; but that all things should be attracted alike by something, whether they happen to be akin in their qualities or most opposite, is full of astonishing absurdity. Thus you have not only admitted attraction, but have done so in a far worse way than you should have, by saying it is not only of what is proper, but simply of everything. And so it seems to me that you deserve to be abused rather than praised by your chorus. And that you have never even used purgative drugs, but are a layman without resources in the works of medicine, I think I shall also show briefly. The drugs whose nature is to purge black bile evacuate black [bile] right from the start. The evacuations differ from one another in that some are more fluid, and those that follow them are always thicker and thicker. This same thing is also the case with those that purge phlegm and yellow bile. For each of them attracts the humour proper to it from the start, but thicker as time goes on; yet it is not, as you suppose, that someone first filled a whole basin with serous residue, then another with yellow bile, and then another with phlegm, and that only then is the black [bile] evacuated. From this it is clear that what is proper to the drug is attracted by it, and that the watery matter floating on the surface follows along with it. And you can observe this now, even if you did not before: that people evacuate a very great quantity of watery and bilious matter upon such doses of drugs, while the whole evacuation they undergo is very small upon those that draw off black [bile]. But on your hypothesis, at any rate, the total evacuated should always have been greatest with those [that draw off] black [bile], and least with the watery and bilious ones. For your argument, I suppose, distinguished the kind of matter evacuated by the weakness and strength of the drugs, as in the case of those that draw off black [bile]. And since these differ from the others in strength, there will be an enormous evacuation, first of all the watery matter, then of the bilious, then of the phlegmatic, then of the black [bile] itself. But with the weak purgatives only the watery matter by itself will be evacuated. Yet none of these things is seen to occur, so that these observed facts overthrow your argument. And you ought also to answer why, if the thicker matter is always evacuated after the thinner, black bile is attracted before blood, although it is a kind of sediment of the blood, like the lees in wines.

Perhaps, then, you will ask whether there is any drug that draws off blood right from the start. There is, my good man, but no one would use it. Why? you will perhaps say. Because that would be to slaughter the person, not to purge him. For purgative drugs are called purgative by everyone for this very reason, that they render the blood pure of the residues mentioned. Surely no doctor is so wise as to wish to evacuate all the blood while leaving the other humours in the body. That is why they count among the deadly poisons all such [drugs] as bring about an evacuation of blood through the veins around the stomach and intestines. Yet on your hypothesis not even these should evacuate blood from the start. As for the names of such drugs, even if I knew them for certain, I would not reveal them in writing. But this alone it is safe for me to tell: what happened among the Bithynian Thracians when we were still boys. A man found a plant of such a kind that whoever took it passed blood and so perished. When many, then, were dying in a similar way, they judged the occurrence worthy of closer inquiry, found the poisoner, and brought him before the governor of the province. When the governor made it his business not only to put the man himself to death, but also anyone else who had either taught him or learned from him, he said that he had learned about the herb from no one, but that once when he was carrying a pig's liver to a suburb, his belly seized up and he put it down on a plant, and then, picking it up again, saw bloody serum flowing out from the whole liver onto the plant; and from this, having conjectured that the plant probably attracted blood, he gave it to some chance person as a trial, and when he found what he had expected, he used it for evil thereafter. But he said that he had not shown the plant to any other person either. This is what that poisoner said under prolonged torture. And the governor of the province, since [the man] had said in the account he gave of the plant that it grew in great abundance everywhere, ordered him to be led away blindfolded to die, so that he might not show it to anyone on the way. So, my good man, it is likely that many drugs have been discovered having such a power as to attract blood right from the start. But it is reasonable that they should be passed over in silence, just as the other deadly poisons are passed over in silence by all who have sense. For there have already been some who were lavish in teaching about these too, displaying a monstrous kind of fellowship and writing out the preparations of each of the deadly poisons; but such men are not among those who have sense, just as neither are you, if you ask us which drugs draw off blood. Let us then bring the argument back again to its original aim. The man who says that all the humours are attracted alike, but that the most free-flowing are separated out first and the others after them, betrays what is dearest to him by admitting that the attractive power exists in things. Over this power his chorus behaves shamelessly, and he has brought himself to say outlandish things about the separation of bile and urine, about distribution, and about other such matters; and furthermore he makes assertions contrary to the observed facts, as we showed earlier. For if this hypothesis is true, the total evacuation will be greatest with those that draw off black [bile], and least with those that draw off serous residues. And yet I will show you ten thousand times, if you are willing, sophist, at least now, to watch the works of the art, that the greatest evacuation always follows hydragogue drugs, and the smallest follows those that purge black [bile]. And I will show too that the black [bile] is evacuated right at the beginning.

So the man who says that all the humours are attracted alike is to this extent insensible and ignorant; and let the man who says they are altered see in turn to what extent, on his view, it will make no difference whether one phlebotomises a jaundiced person or purges him with a cholagogue drug. In the same way it is all one to phlebotomise a person with dropsy and to evacuate him with one of the hydragogues. Then are such things not shameful? The many, hearing such things when doctors contradict one another, laugh at them, not rightly, and all condemn reasoned argument, and call those who utter anything at all *logiatroi* [word-doctors]. For what I am always in the habit of saying, it is the right moment for me to say now too: any layman is better than such a sophist. For even if nothing else, laymen at least preserve their natural notions, whereas the sophists destroy even these through bad habits. Recently, at any rate, a layman of some sense, when eruptions suddenly appeared on many parts of his body, ulcerous and of a bad colour, went to the doctor, asking to be purged as quickly as possible. And when the doctor told him rather to be phlebotomised, "Don't be mad," he said; "for it stands to reason that what is good would be evacuated along with what is corrupted." But those who wish anything rather than that the Hippocratic doctrine be true destroy even the common notions besides, through their love of strife. And then they leap upon us as though to tear us apart, and are annoyed at refutations by the deeds themselves. But it would be just that, as we bear with them when they mean to insult Hippocrates over what they do not understand, and try to persuade them, so they too should endure refutations, and above all, if possible, feel affection for those who have taught them; and if not, at least by no means hate them. One of the doctors of such stupidity, at any rate, on hearing that I had treated a great many people by purging alone, namely those with what are called *alopeciai* [fox-mange, hair loss], began from then on to hate me. And another hated me likewise because [I had treated by purging alone] incipient cancerous conditions, the so-called elephants, and *phagedainai* [spreading ulcers], and many other malignant ulcers; another because I had treated people with vertigo by purgings alone; another because I had cured people who were manic, epileptic and melancholic, and also not a few who suffered from chronic headache, by purgings alone, as also people with sciatica. So too [I cured] chronic pains scattered over many places, and this man recently who had already been treated by the doctors for three months as a case of colic and was getting worse: I told him to throw all those things away and cured him by purgings alone. I also cured a female flux in a not undistinguished woman at Rome by purgings alone, as also in many other, less distinguished women both this same affection and certain others that arise in the womb. As for erysipelas, why need I even say that no remedy is more effective than a cholagogue drug, just as the one that draws off phlegm is most opposed to it? I could go on for a whole day telling of other marvellous results that follow purgings, of which those who have never learned the art of purgative drugs are likely to be ignorant. For where they do not even believe that there is any purgative drug at all, how, I ask, will they know in which cases it should be used, or in what manner? For this reason others treat affections guided by bare experience alone. But these wise men of ours also take up reasoned argument, not so as to add something to what has been found through experience, but to overturn even that, and they practise medicine far worse than those who set out from bare, irrational routine alone. Of all this there is one beginning and source, hatred of Hippocrates; and from this source flowed many other things, and also this very inquiry now before us, the one concerning the attractive power, of which the power of purgative drugs is a part or kind, or whatever one may wish to call it.
